title: Forces of Nature
summary: Work out Coulomb forces, weigh electric against gravity, count the electrons in a coulomb and test charge conservation.
subject: physics
concepts: The size of a coulomb and quantisation
learningOutcome: The student can find a Coulomb force or distance, compare electric and gravitational forces, count electrons in a charge, show the mass moved is negligible, and test charge conservation.

levels.title: Force between two charges
levels.adds: Baseline: F = kq₁q₂/r² for the force or the distance, and equal and opposite forces on the two charges (Ex 1.1, 1.2).
hints: Convert µC to coulombs and cm to metres before using k = 9 × 10⁹ N m²/C².
To find the distance, rearrange: r = √(k q₁ q₂ / F).
The two spheres push on each other with forces of equal size and opposite direction.

levels.title: Electric against gravity
levels.adds: New idea: the electric force between particles is about 10³⁶ times the gravitational force (Ex 1.3, Example 1.3).
hints: Divide k q² / r² by G m₁ m₂ / r²: the distance cancels.
Use the proton mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and electron mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
Gravity still rules planets because electric forces cancel: charges come in both signs.

levels.title: How big is a coulomb?
levels.adds: New idea: a coulomb is about 6 × 10¹⁸ electrons, so charge looks continuous at ordinary scales (Example 1.1, Ex 1.4b).
hints: The number of electrons is N = q / e with e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Charge gathered each second = rate × e. Divide 1 C by it for the time in seconds.
One electron is a tiny step compared with the whole charge, so quantisation is invisible.

levels.title: The mass of charging
levels.adds: New idea: charging moves electrons, from one body to the other, and the mass they carry is negligible (Ex 1.11).
hints: N = q / e, and the mass moved is N times the mass of one electron.
A body that ends up negative has gained electrons; one that ends up positive has lost them.
The mass is far too small to ever measure.

levels.title: Conservation checker
levels.adds: New idea: charge is conserved in every process: the total before equals the total after (Ex 1.5).
hints: Add up the charges on each side of every collision, in units of e.
Neutral particles (neutron, neutrino, photon) carry zero charge.
If the two totals differ, charge would be created or destroyed: forbidden.

misconceptions: The force on the lighter charge is smaller
Gravity is stronger than the electric force
Charge is not quantised for big objects
Charging a body makes it measurably heavier
Charge can be created in a collision
